title: What Do We Get from Two-Way Fixed Effects Regressions? Implications from Numerical Equivalence
abstract: This paper develops numerical and causal interpretations of two-way fixed effects (TWFE) regressions, allowing for general scalar treatments with non-staggered designs and time-varying covariates. Building on the numerical equivalence between TWFE and pooled first-difference regressions, I decompose the TWFE coefficient into a weighted average of first-difference coefficients across varying horizons, clarifying contributions of short-run versus long-run changes. Causal interpretation of the TWFE coefficient requires common trends assumptions for all time horizons, conditional on changes, not levels, of time-varying covariates. I develop diagnostic procedures to assess this assumption's plausibility across different horizons, extending beyond recent literature's focus on binary, staggered treatments.
gemini_output:
\noindent\textbf{1. BACKGROUND \& CONTEXT}\\
This research critically examines Two-Way Fixed Effects (TWFE) regressions, a widely used statistical method in fields from economics to public health, to understand what they truly measure. It provides both numerical and causal interpretations, especially for complex scenarios involving scalar treatments, non-staggered designs, and time-varying covariates, moving beyond simpler applications. Understanding TWFE's underlying mechanics is vital because misinterpretations can lead to flawed policy decisions and incorrect scientific conclusions, underscoring the need for clarity in causal inference.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{2. REAL-WORLD PROBLEMS SOLVED}\\
The paper addresses the common problem of misinterpreting the causal effects estimated by TWFE regressions, particularly when treatment effects are heterogeneous or the study design is complex. It solves this by decomposing the TWFE coefficient into a weighted average of first-difference coefficients across various time horizons, revealing contributions from both short-run and long-run changes. This decomposition clarifies that reliable causal inference requires common trends assumptions across all time horizons, conditional on *changes* in covariates, not just their levels. At TRL 2 (concept formulated), this theoretical work offers diagnostic procedures to improve the validity of applied research.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{3. MARKET ANALYSIS}\\
The primary market for this research is within academic institutions, policy-making bodies, and data analytics firms that extensively use causal inference methods. There is high demand among researchers, economists, and social scientists who rely on TWFE regressions for policy evaluation and impact assessment. Adoption challenges include integrating these new diagnostic procedures into existing statistical software and shifting established analytical practices. While no direct competitors offer this specific decomposition, the work complements existing econometric tools. Collaborations with statistical software developers (e.g., R, Python, Stata communities) are key to disseminating and integrating these advanced diagnostics.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{4. IMMEDIATE IDEAS FOR STARTUPS/PATENTS}\\
This research is unlikely to be patentable as it constitutes a methodological advancement in statistical theory rather than a new invention. However, it offers significant value for quantum software development and existing data analytics platforms. Startups or established firms focused on econometric software could develop and license packages or modules that implement these diagnostic procedures, helping users validate their TWFE assumptions. A viable standalone startup focused solely on this insight is improbable. A practical next step is the development of open-source R or Python packages, or commercial add-ons for statistical software, to empower researchers with these new diagnostic capabilities.

title: The infinite information gap between mathematical and physical representations
abstract: Partial orders have been used to model several experimental setups, going from classical thermodynamics and general relativity to the quantum realm with its resource theories. In order to study such experimental setups, one typically characterizes them via a (numerical) representation, that is, a set of real-valued functions. In the context of resource theory, it is customary to use \textbf{mathematical} representations, i.e. a set of \textbf{measurement outcomes} which characterize the achievable transitions within the experimental setup. However, in line with the minimum energy and maximum entropy principles in classical mechanics and thermodynamics, respectively, one would expect an optimization interpretation for a representation to be called \textbf{physical}. More specifically, a physical representation could consist of a set of competing \textbf{optimization principles} such that a transition happens provided they are all optimized by it. Somewhat surprisingly, we show that this distinction can result in an \textbf{infinite information gap}, with some partial orders having mathematical representations that involve a finite amount of information and requiring infinite information to build a physical representation. We connect this phenomenon with well-known resource-theoretic scenarios like majorization, and develop notions of partial order dimension that run in parallel to the representations that we consider. Our results improve on the classification of preordered spaces in terms of real-valued functions.
gemini_output:
\noindent\textbf{1. BACKGROUND \& CONTEXT}\\
This research explores how we characterize and understand experimental setups, ranging from classical physics to quantum resource theories, using "partial orders." Traditionally, these systems are described by a set of real-valued functions, called "representations." The study differentiates between "mathematical representations" (based on measurable outcomes) and "physical representations" (derived from underlying optimization principles like minimum energy). This distinction is critical because it uncovers fundamental differences in how we model and interpret transformations within these systems, which has significant implications for understanding the true capabilities of various physical processes.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{2. REAL-WORLD PROBLEMS SOLVED}\\
The paper addresses a critical conceptual problem: the potential for an "infinite information gap" between mathematical and physical descriptions of a system. It proves that some partial orders, while describable by finite mathematical information (measurement outcomes), paradoxically require infinite information for a truly physical representation (optimization principles). This reveals that simply measuring outcomes might not capture the full, underlying physical reality or constraints of a system. At TRL 1 (basic principles observed and reported), this theoretical insight prevents misinterpretations in fields like quantum resource theory, where understanding what transformations are physically possible is paramount.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{3. MARKET ANALYSIS}\\
While highly theoretical, this research provides foundational insights for the emerging quantum computing and information market, particularly in quantum resource theory. There isn't a direct product market, but demand exists for rigorous theoretical frameworks that underpin quantum algorithm design and experimental validation. The work challenges assumptions about the completeness of certain system characterizations, influencing developers of quantum software and researchers working on resource-efficient quantum protocols. Adoption challenges include the abstract nature of the work, but its value lies in preventing future design flaws. Collaborations with academic groups and quantum research labs focused on foundational physics are the most immediate path forward.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{4. IMMEDIATE IDEAS FOR STARTUPS/PATENTS}\\
This fundamental mathematical finding is unpatentable as it exposes inherent properties rather than inventing a device or process. Similarly, a standalone startup based on this diagnosis is unlikely. However, the insights are crucial for quantum software development and theoretical modeling. Companies designing quantum simulation tools or quantum resource management platforms could integrate these findings to ensure their models accurately reflect physical limitations. A practical next step would be to develop formal validation frameworks or diagnostic tools that flag potential "information gaps" when characterizing quantum resource theories or designing protocols based on partial orders, guiding more physically accurate implementations.

title: Jihad over Centuries
abstract: This paper examines the origins of Islamist insurgencies, or jihad, through the lens of past prosperity, decline, and cultural revival in West Africa. Using shrinking water sources as an instrument, we show that trans-Saharan cities once-thriving under pre-colonial Islamic states but now deserted have become contemporary hotspots of jihadist violence. We argue that military power asymmetries between Islamic states and colonizers during historical jihad shaped the persistence of jihadist ideology, fueling today's resurgence especially in areas that lacked intense armed resistance against colonial invasions. Extensive qualitative evidence, a dynamic model of conflict, and individual-level surveys examining ideologies support this mechanism.
gemini_output:
\noindent\textbf{1. BACKGROUND \& CONTEXT}\\
This research delves into the historical origins of Islamist insurgencies, known as jihad, by examining patterns of past prosperity, decline, and cultural revival in West Africa. The study is critical for understanding why contemporary jihadist violence is prevalent in specific regions, using shrinking water sources as a unique historical instrument to link past economic conditions to current conflict hotspots. Key concepts include pre-colonial Islamic states, the impact of colonial invasions, and the persistence of jihadist ideology, providing a novel historical lens on modern conflict dynamics.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{2. REAL-WORLD PROBLEMS SOLVED}\\
The paper clarifies why modern jihadist violence disproportionately affects areas that were once-thriving Islamic cities but are now deserted. It proves that military power imbalances during historical colonial resistance shaped the endurance of jihadist ideology, particularly fueling its resurgence in regions that mounted less intense armed resistance against colonial invaders. At TRL 2 (concept formulated), this theoretical insight offers a crucial framework for understanding the geographical persistence of conflict. Advancing requires integrating these findings into contemporary conflict prevention strategies and policy-making.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{3. MARKET ANALYSIS}\\
The market for understanding and mitigating conflict is significant, primarily serving governments, NGOs, and international security organizations. Demand exists for data-driven insights into the root causes of instability, particularly in regions like West Africa. This research offers a unique, historically informed perspective that differentiates it from purely contemporary analyses. Adoption challenges include the political sensitivity of historical narratives and the integration of academic insights into actionable policy. Collaborations with conflict resolution think tanks or governmental agencies could accelerate the application of these findings.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{4. IMMEDIATE IDEAS FOR STARTUPS/PATENTS}\\
The research itself is unpatentable, as it provides a historical analysis and theoretical framework rather than an invention. However, it can inform the development of risk assessment tools for conflict-prone regions. Startups or specialized consultancies could leverage these insights to offer strategic intelligence or predictive analytics to governments and aid organizations, helping identify areas most vulnerable to future insurgencies based on historical factors. A viable next step involves developing policy recommendations and training programs for diplomats and security personnel working in West Africa, emphasizing the long-term historical drivers of conflict.

title: The Arrival of Fast Internet and Employment in Africa: Comment
abstract: Hjort and Poulsen (2019) frames the staggered arrival of submarine Internet cables on the shores of Africa circa 2010 as a difference-in-differences natural experiment. The paper finds positive impacts of broadband on individual- and firm-level employment -- with a bias toward skilled employment -- and on nighttime light emissions. These results largely are not robust to alternative geocoding of survey locations, to correcting for a satellite changeover at end-2009, and to revisiting a definition of the treated zone that has no clear technological basis, is narrower than the spatial resolution of nearly all the data sources, and is empirically suboptimal as a representation of the geography of broadband.
gemini_output:
\noindent\textbf{1. BACKGROUND \& CONTEXT}\\
This research critically re-evaluates a previous study by Hjort and Poulsen (2019) that examined the economic impact of fast internet in Africa. The original study used the arrival of submarine internet cables around 2010 as a "natural experiment," claiming significant positive effects of broadband on employment (especially skilled jobs) and overall economic activity, indicated by nighttime light emissions. This new analysis is crucial because it challenges the robustness of these findings, suggesting the initial conclusions might be unreliable. It highlights the importance of rigorous methodology when assessing the real-world impact of major infrastructure developments.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{2. REAL-WORLD PROBLEMS SOLVED}\\
The paper addresses the significant problem of potentially flawed evidence informing policy decisions, particularly concerning investment in digital infrastructure for development. It demonstrates that the prior findings, suggesting fast internet drives employment growth in Africa, are not robust when re-examined using alternative data treatment, geocoding, and a more appropriate definition of internet-affected areas. By uncovering these methodological weaknesses, this research prevents misdirected investments and policies based on inaccurate economic impact assessments. At TRL 2 (concept formulated through critical re-analysis), this work emphasizes the need for meticulous data validation in development economics. Advancing this requires widespread adoption of more rigorous analytical standards in policy-relevant studies.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{3. MARKET ANALYSIS}\\
The "market" for this research is primarily within the spheres of policy-making, international development, and economic research, where there is a strong demand for reliable data on the impact of internet access in emerging economies. This work highlights a crucial unmet need: robust, independently verified economic impact studies. It competes indirectly with less rigorous research by raising the bar for evidence quality. While there are no direct regulatory hurdles, the findings influence how development agencies and governments allocate resources for digital inclusion. Collaboration with data science organizations or policy evaluation firms could help standardize the adoption of these rigorous analytical approaches.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{4. IMMEDIATE IDEAS FOR STARTUPS/PATENTS}\\
This research itself is unpatentable, as it is a critical re-analysis exposing methodological limitations rather than an invention. However, it strongly informs the need for specialized data validation and geospatial analysis services within economic research and development. A viable startup could emerge offering "economic impact auditing" services, where expert teams critically review methodologies, data integrity, and spatial modeling for large-scale development projects for government bodies, NGOs, or investment firms. Such a service would ensure that policy recommendations are built on sound evidence. A practical next step involves integrating these methodological critiques into best practices for evaluating development interventions, fostering demand for such specialized analytical support.

title: Distributional Treatment Effect with Latent Rank Invariance
abstract: Treatment effect heterogeneity is of a great concern when evaluating policy impact: "is the treatment Pareto-improving?", "what is the proportion of people who are better off under the treatment?", etc. However, even in the simple case of a binary random treatment, existing analysis has been mostly limited to an average treatment effect or a quantile treatment effect, due to the fundamental limitation that we cannot simultaneously observe both treated potential outcome and untreated potential outcome for a given unit. This paper assumes a conditional independence assumption that the two potential outcomes are independent of each other given a scalar latent variable. With a specific example of strictly increasing conditional expectation, I label the latent variable as 'latent rank' and motivate the identifying assumption as 'latent rank invariance.' In implementation, I assume a finite support on the latent variable and propose an estimation strategy based on a nonnegative matrix factorization. A limiting distribution is derived for the distributional treatment effect estimator, using Neyman orthogonality.
gemini_output:
\noindent\textbf{1. BACKGROUND \& CONTEXT}\\
This research offers a novel approach to understanding how treatments or policies affect different individuals, moving beyond simple average outcomes. It investigates "distributional treatment effects," which reveal the full spectrum of impacts—who benefits, who is unaffected, and who might be worse off. The study is critical because traditional methods often only provide an average effect, masking important variations in impact due to the fundamental challenge of not observing both treated and untreated outcomes for the same person. This work proposes a "latent rank invariance" assumption, using a scalar latent variable and nonnegative matrix factorization, to overcome this limitation and provide a more granular view of policy efficacy.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{2. REAL-WORLD PROBLEMS SOLVED}\\
The paper addresses the inability of current policy evaluations to answer crucial questions about individual-level impact, such as whether a policy is "Pareto-improving" (benefiting some without harming others) or the exact proportion of people who are better off. By introducing a method to estimate the full distribution of treatment effects, this research allows policymakers to understand the nuanced, heterogeneous consequences of interventions. At TRL 2 (concept formulated), this theoretical framework provides a vital tool for assessing equity and efficiency in diverse fields from healthcare to social welfare programs, moving beyond generalized insights to specific population segments.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{3. MARKET ANALYSIS}\\
The market for advanced policy evaluation and impact assessment is significant, encompassing government agencies, NGOs, and corporations implementing large-scale interventions. There is strong demand for more precise tools to measure the effectiveness of social programs, medical treatments, and marketing campaigns, driven by calls for evidence-based decision-making. While existing methods offer average or quantile effects, this research carves out a niche by providing a comprehensive distributional view. Adoption challenges include the need for specialized econometric expertise and integration into current data analytics workflows, but the unique insights offered could be highly valuable for targeted policy design.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{4. IMMEDIATE IDEAS FOR STARTUPS/PATENTS}\\
While the core econometric theory is unlikely patentable, the specific estimation strategy involving nonnegative matrix factorization and its implementation could be part of a proprietary software solution. A viable startup could develop a specialized software platform or offer consulting services focused on applying "latent rank invariance" for detailed policy impact assessment. Such a tool would enable organizations to easily analyze treatment effect heterogeneity, offering a competitive edge over conventional evaluation methods. A practical next step involves creating an open-source or commercial software library that allows researchers and practitioners to seamlessly integrate this method into their existing data analysis pipelines.

title: From Predictive Algorithms to Automatic Generation of Anomalies
abstract: How can we extract theoretical insights from machine learning algorithms? We take a familiar lesson: researchers often turn their intuitions into theoretical insights by constructing "anomalies" -- specific examples highlighting hypothesized flaws in a theory, such as the Allais paradox and the Kahneman-Tversky choice experiments for expected utility. We develop procedures that replace researchers' intuitions with predictive algorithms: given a predictive algorithm and a theory, our procedures automatically generate anomalies for that theory. We illustrate our procedures with a concrete application: generating anomalies for expected utility theory. Based on a neural network that accurately predicts lottery choices, our procedures recover known anomalies for expected utility theory and discover new ones absent from existing work. In incentivized experiments, subjects violate expected utility theory on these algorithmically generated anomalies at rates similar to the Allais paradox and common ratio effect.
gemini_output:
\noindent\textbf{1. BACKGROUND \& CONTEXT}\\
This research introduces a novel approach to scientific discovery, focusing on how machine learning can automate the identification of flaws in established theories. Historically, researchers have refined theories by constructing "anomalies"—specific examples that highlight where a theory fails to predict outcomes, such as the Allais paradox in economics. This study proposes replacing human intuition with predictive algorithms to automatically generate such anomalies. It is crucial because it offers a systematic, data-driven method to accelerate the refinement and improvement of theoretical models across various scientific disciplines.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{2. REAL-WORLD PROBLEMS SOLVED}\\
The paper addresses the challenge that discovering conceptual flaws in theories often relies on subjective human intuition, making the process slow, inconsistent, and limited. It solves this by developing procedures that, given a predictive algorithm and a theory, automatically generate anomalies for that theory. Applied to Expected Utility Theory (EUT) and trained on lottery choices, these procedures not only rediscover known EUT anomalies but also uncover new ones previously unobserved. At TRL 3 (experimental proof of concept), this method provides a powerful tool to rigorously test and improve theoretical models by systematically exposing their limitations. Advancing requires applying this automated anomaly generation to a broader range of scientific theories.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{3. MARKET ANALYSIS}\\
The market for this research lies primarily within academic institutions, scientific research labs, and potentially within AI development teams focused on robust model validation. Demand exists from researchers across fields like economics, psychology, and social sciences who need to test and refine their theoretical frameworks. Adoption challenges include integrating these new AI-driven tools into traditional research methodologies and building trust in algorithmically generated insights. While there are no direct competitors offering automated anomaly generation, existing statistical methods and human expert review serve as indirect alternatives. Collaborations with academic publishers or research software providers could accelerate market penetration by offering this as a validation service.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{4. IMMEDIATE IDEAS FOR STARTUPS/PATENTS}\\
The core methodology—the procedure for automatically generating anomalies using predictive algorithms to critique theories—is potentially patentable as a novel AI-driven scientific discovery tool. A viable startup could develop a software platform or API allowing researchers to input their predictive models and theories to automatically generate validation test cases. This tool could be licensed to universities, research organizations, or even companies building complex AI systems that require rigorous theoretical grounding and validation. A practical next step is to develop a user-friendly prototype demonstrating its application across several diverse theories, beyond just expected utility, to showcase its broad utility.

title: Canonical correlation analysis of stochastic trends via functional approximation
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach for semiparametric inference on the number $s$ of common trends and their loading matrix $ψ$ in $I(1)/I(0)$ systems. It combines functional approximation of limits of random walks and canonical correlations analysis, performed between the $p$ observed time series of length $T$ and the first $K$ discretized elements of an $L^2$ basis. Tests and selection criteria on $s$, and estimators and tests on $ψ$ are proposed; their properties are discussed as $T$ and $K$ diverge sequentially for fixed $p$ and $s$. It is found that tests on $s$ are asymptotically pivotal, selection criteria of $s$ are consistent, estimators of $ψ$ are $T$-consistent, mixed-Gaussian and efficient, so that Wald tests on $ψ$ are asymptotically Normal or $χ^2$. The paper also discusses asymptotically pivotal misspecification tests for checking model assumptions. The approach can be coherently applied to subsets or aggregations of variables in a given panel. Monte Carlo simulations show that these tools have reasonable performance for $T\geq 10 p$ and $p\leq 300$. An empirical analysis of 20 exchange rates illustrates the methods.
gemini_output:
\noindent\textbf{1. BACKGROUND \& CONTEXT}\\
This research introduces a new method to identify and analyze long-term patterns, or "stochastic trends," in time-series data, common in economics and finance. It's crucial for understanding how many fundamental, persistent drivers influence complex systems, like how many underlying factors determine exchange rates. The study combines functional approximation of random walks with canonical correlation analysis, offering a more robust way to uncover these trends and their "loading matrix"—how much each trend affects observed variables. This novel approach provides a theoretically sound framework for semiparametric inference on these persistent features, improving upon existing techniques for analyzing integrated and cointegrated systems.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{2. REAL-WORLD PROBLEMS SOLVED}\\
The paper addresses the challenge of accurately determining the number and impact of common trends in dynamic datasets, where traditional methods can struggle with noise and complex interdependencies. For example, in financial markets, identifying underlying economic trends is vital for forecasting and risk management. This research proves that its proposed tests for the number of trends are asymptotically pivotal, and estimators for their loading are efficient, meaning they are more reliable and precise. At TRL 2-3 (concept formulated and analytically validated), this offers a robust statistical tool for economists and quantitative analysts, clarifying how to extract meaningful, long-term signals from noisy, high-dimensional time-series data.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{3. MARKET ANALYSIS}\\
The market for advanced econometric and time-series analysis tools is significant within quantitative finance, macroeconomic forecasting, and data science. There's demand for robust methods that can handle large datasets and provide reliable insights into market dynamics and economic indicators. This research offers a competitive edge over existing cointegration methods by providing a semiparametric, more flexible framework. Adoption challenges include the need for integration into popular statistical software packages (e.g., R, Python) and educating users on its theoretical advantages. Collaborations with financial data providers or analytics firms could accelerate its market penetration by demonstrating its practical superiority for tasks like asset allocation or policy analysis.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{4. IMMEDIATE IDEAS FOR STARTUPS/PATENTS}\\
The core mathematical methodology is unlikely to be patentable, as it is a theoretical statistical framework. However, the unique implementation of this approach in software could be valuable. A viable path for a startup would involve developing and commercializing a specialized software library or API that efficiently applies this method, particularly optimized for large-scale financial or economic datasets. Such a tool could be licensed to quantitative hedge funds, investment banks, or central banks for improved forecasting and risk modeling. A practical next step is to create an open-source (or commercial) package, rigorously document its use, and demonstrate its performance on diverse real-world datasets beyond the 20 exchange rates, possibly leading to a consulting service specializing in advanced trend analysis.

title: Efficient Major Transition Exchange under Distributional and Dual Priority-respecting Constraints
abstract: Many real matching markets encounter distributional and fairness constraints. Motivated by the Chinese Major Transition Program (CMT), this paper studies the design of exchange mechanisms within a fresh framework of both distributional and dual priority-respecting constraints. Specifically, each student has an initial assigned major and applies to transfer to a more desirable one. A student can successfully transfer majors only if they obtain eligibility from both their initial major and the applied major. Each major has a dual priority: a strict priority over current students who wish to transfer out and a strict priority over students from other majors who wish to transfer in. Additionally, each major faces a ceiling constraint and a floor constraint to regulate student distribution. We show that the existing mechanisms of CMT result in avoidable inefficiencies, and propose two mechanisms that can match students to majors in an efficient way as well as respecting each major's distributional and dual priority. The efficient mechanisms are based on a proposed solution concept: eligibility maximization (EM), and two processes for identifying improvement cycles--specifically, transfer-in exchangeable cycles and transfer-out exchangeable cycles.
gemini_output:
\noindent\textbf{1. BACKGROUND \& CONTEXT}\\
This research focuses on designing efficient systems for allocating students to academic majors, particularly when students wish to transfer. The study is important because many real-world matching scenarios, such as university major transitions, require balancing student preferences with institutional rules, often involving complex constraints like major capacities and specific priority systems. It explores a new framework motivated by China's Major Transition Program (CMT), where students apply to transfer majors based on eligibility from both their current and desired major, and majors hold "dual priorities" over transferring students. Understanding these dynamics is key to developing fair and efficient allocation mechanisms in educational and other resource-constrained settings.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{2. REAL-WORLD PROBLEMS SOLVED}\\
The paper directly addresses inefficiencies found in existing major transition programs, like the CMT, where current mechanisms often fail to achieve optimal student placements. This means students might not be assigned to their most preferred major, even when a feasible, better transfer option exists within the rules. The research proposes two novel mechanisms, built on an "eligibility maximization" concept and specific cycle-identifying processes, that effectively resolve these inefficiencies. At TRL 2 (concept formulated and validated through theoretical analysis), this work provides practical solutions that ensure students are matched to majors in a way that respects all complex distributional and priority constraints while maximizing overall transfer efficiency.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{3. MARKET ANALYSIS}\\
The primary market for this research lies within educational institutions, specifically universities and colleges that manage complex student major allocation and transfer processes. There is significant demand for systems that improve student satisfaction, optimize resource utilization (major capacities), and streamline administrative burdens associated with transfers. While a niche market, efficient allocation tools are valuable as institutions seek to enhance student experience and operational efficiency. Adoption challenges may include integrating with legacy university information systems and overcoming resistance to changing established administrative procedures. However, the clear benefits of improved efficiency and fairness offer strong potential for market entry.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{4. IMMEDIATE IDEAS FOR STARTUPS/PATENTS}\\
While the underlying mathematical insights may not be directly patentable, the specific mechanisms and algorithms developed could be incorporated into proprietary software. A viable startup could emerge by developing a specialized software platform for university administration. This platform would enable institutions to configure their unique major capacities, dual priority rules, and student eligibility criteria, then apply these efficient matching algorithms to automate and optimize major transfers. This solution could be licensed to universities to replace or enhance their current, often inefficient, manual or ad-hoc systems. A practical next step would involve developing a prototype and piloting it with a university to demonstrate its tangible benefits in student satisfaction and administrative cost reduction.

title: Bayesian Model Averaging in Causal Instrumental Variable Models
abstract: Instrumental variables are a popular tool to infer causal effects under unobserved confounding, but choosing suitable instruments is challenging in practice. We propose gIVBMA, a Bayesian model averaging procedure that addresses this challenge by averaging across different sets of instrumental variables and covariates in a structural equation model. Our approach extends previous work through a scale-invariant prior structure and accommodates non-Gaussian outcomes and treatments, offering greater flexibility than existing methods. The computational strategy uses conditional Bayes factors to update models separately for the outcome and treatments. We prove that this model selection procedure is consistent. By explicitly accounting for model uncertainty, gIVBMA allows instruments and covariates to switch roles and provides robustness against invalid instruments. In simulation experiments, gIVBMA outperforms current state-of-the-art methods. We demonstrate its usefulness in two empirical applications: the effects of malaria and institutions on income per capita and the returns to schooling. A software implementation of gIVBMA is available in Julia.
gemini_output:
\noindent\textbf{1. BACKGROUND \& CONTEXT}\\
This research introduces gIVBMA, a new method for inferring causal effects using instrumental variables, which are essential for understanding cause-and-effect relationships when other factors are unknown. The study is important because choosing the right instrumental variables is a major challenge, leading to unreliable conclusions. gIVBMA addresses this by systematically averaging across different sets of potential instruments and other variables within a structural equation model. This approach improves upon existing methods by being more flexible, handling various types of data, and providing more robust causal estimates.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{2. REAL-WORLD PROBLEMS SOLVED}\\
The paper solves the critical problem of unreliable causal inference in fields like economics, public health, and social sciences, where unobserved factors can skew results. By using Bayesian model averaging, gIVBMA robustly accounts for the uncertainty in selecting appropriate instrumental variables, which is akin to finding the right lens to view a complex problem. This ensures that the estimated causal effects are less prone to errors from invalid instruments or model misspecification. At TRL 3-4 (experimental validation in empirical applications), this method offers a more trustworthy tool for policy-makers and researchers. Advancing requires integrating this method into widely used statistical software.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{3. MARKET ANALYSIS}\\
The market for robust causal inference methods is substantial, spanning academic research, government policy analysis, and data-driven industries. Demand exists for tools that can provide more reliable insights from complex observational data. While various instrumental variable methods exist, gIVBMA offers a unique advantage through its explicit handling of model uncertainty and flexibility with non-Gaussian data. Adoption challenges include the need for users to understand its Bayesian framework and integrate the Julia-based software into existing workflows. Collaborations with analytics firms or specialized consultancies could accelerate market penetration.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{4. IMMEDIATE IDEAS FOR STARTUPS/PATENTS}\\
The statistical method itself is unlikely to be patentable in isolation. However, the practical application of gIVBMA offers commercial potential. A startup could develop specialized software packages or modules (building on the existing Julia implementation) that integrate gIVBMA into platforms used by economists, epidemiologists, or policy analysts, focusing on specific industry verticals (e.g., healthcare outcomes, education policy). Another avenue is a consultancy service providing expert causal inference analysis using gIVBMA for clients across various sectors. The next step is to create user-friendly interfaces and comprehensive training for the method, targeting wider professional adoption.

title: A primal-dual price-optimization method for computing equilibrium prices in mean-field games models
abstract: We develop a simple yet efficient Lagrangian method for computing equilibrium prices in a mean-field game price-formation model. We prove that equilibrium prices are optimal in terms of a suitable criterion and derive a primal-dual gradient-based algorithm for computing them. One of the highlights of our computational framework is the efficient, simple, and flexible implementation of the algorithm using modern automatic differentiation techniques. Our implementation is modular and admits a seamless extension to high-dimensional settings with more complex dynamics, costs, and equilibrium conditions. Additionally, automatic differentiation enables a versatile algorithm that requires only coding the cost functions of agents. It automatically handles the gradients of the costs, thereby eliminating the need to manually form the adjoint equations.
gemini_output:
\noindent\textbf{1. BACKGROUND \& CONTEXT}\\
This research introduces an efficient method for calculating equilibrium prices within "mean-field game" (MFG) models, which describe systems with many interacting agents. The study is important because MFGs are complex, and finding stable prices is computationally challenging. This work develops a primal-dual Lagrangian approach, proving that these equilibrium prices are optimal under specific criteria. Key to its efficiency is the use of automatic differentiation, which simplifies the process of handling complex calculations and makes the method flexible for various scenarios.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{2. REAL-WORLD PROBLEMS SOLVED}\\
The paper tackles the difficulty of accurately and efficiently determining stable prices in large-scale systems where individual agents' decisions collectively impact the market—a problem common in fields like energy markets, financial modeling, or supply chain logistics. It provides a computational framework that can scale to high-dimensional problems with complex dynamics without requiring manual, labor-intensive derivations of adjoint equations. At TRL 2-3 (concept formulated and analytically proven with a computational framework), this method offers a practical solution to a significant computational bottleneck. Further development requires testing its performance against real-world datasets or complex simulated environments.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{3. MARKET ANALYSIS}\\
The market for advanced optimization tools in areas like energy grids, financial trading, and dynamic pricing is growing, driven by the need for more sophisticated predictive and prescriptive analytics. This method offers a robust way to model and optimize pricing in systems with numerous interacting participants. While the immediate market for raw MFG solutions is niche, the demand for underlying computational efficiency and scalability is high. Competitors include existing numerical optimization techniques, but this work stands out due to its flexible implementation via automatic differentiation. Regulatory hurdles are minimal, though adoption will depend on integrating into existing industry software stacks.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{4. IMMEDIATE IDEAS FOR STARTUPS/PATENTS}\\
While the mathematical principles might not be patentable, the specific algorithm and its unique implementation, especially leveraging automatic differentiation for MFG equilibrium price computation, could potentially be patented as a novel software method. A practical next step involves building a proof-of-concept software library and demonstrating its efficiency on a targeted industry problem.

title: Anytime-Valid Inference in Adaptive Experiments: Covariate Adjustment and Balanced Power
abstract: Adaptive experiments such as multi-armed bandits offer efficiency gains over traditional randomized experiments but pose two major challenges: invalid inference on the Average Treatment Effect (ATE) due to adaptive sampling and low statistical power for sub-optimal treatments. We address both issues by extending the Mixture Adaptive Design framework (arXiv:2311.05794). First, we propose MADCovar, a covariate-adjusted ATE estimator that is unbiased and preserves anytime-valid inference guarantees while substantially improving ATE precision. Second, we introduce MADMod, which dynamically reallocates samples to underpowered arms, enabling more balanced statistical power across treatments without sacrificing valid inference. Both methods retain MAD's core advantage of constructing asymptotic confidence sequences (CSs) that allow researchers to continuously monitor ATE estimates and stop data collection once a desired precision or significance criterion is met. Empirically, we validate both methods using simulations and real-world data. In simulations, MADCovar reduces CS width by up to $60\%$ relative to MAD. In a large-scale political RCT with $\approx32,000$ participants, MADCovar achieves similar precision gains. MADMod improves statistical power and inferential precision across all treatment arms, particularly for suboptimal treatments. Simulations show that MADMod sharply reduces Type II error while preserving the efficiency benefits of adaptive allocation. Together, MADCovar and MADMod make adaptive experiments more practical, reliable, and efficient for applied researchers across many domains. Our proposed methods are implemented through an open-source software package.
gemini_output:
\noindent\textbf{1. BACKGROUND \& CONTEXT}\\
This research addresses how to improve the reliability and efficiency of adaptive experiments, such as those used in A/B testing or clinical trials, which dynamically adjust resource allocation during the experiment. While these experiments are highly efficient, they often compromise the statistical validity of results and can undersample less successful options. The study extends the Mixture Adaptive Design (MAD) framework to ensure that results remain statistically sound and provide adequate data for all treatments. It's crucial because it allows researchers to leverage adaptive efficiency without sacrificing the trustworthiness of their conclusions.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{2. REAL-WORLD PROBLEMS SOLVED}\\
The paper tackles two critical issues with adaptive experiments: invalid inference on the Average Treatment Effect (ATE) and low statistical power for suboptimal treatments. It introduces MADCovar, a method that provides unbiased, continuously valid ATE estimates with significantly improved precision, effectively making results more reliable. Additionally, MADMod dynamically reallocates samples to ensure sufficient data for all treatment options, not just the best one, increasing overall statistical power. These advancements mean that practitioners in fields like marketing, medicine, or social sciences can conduct more practical, efficient, and trustworthy experiments, leading to faster and more accurate decision-making.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{3. MARKET ANALYSIS}\\
The market for robust, efficient experimental design and data analysis is substantial, encompassing digital marketing, e-commerce, healthcare, and public policy. Companies engaged in continuous optimization and A/B testing face a constant need for methods that deliver rapid insights without sacrificing statistical rigor. This research directly addresses these needs by enhancing the utility of adaptive experiments, making them a more appealing and reliable alternative to traditional fixed-design trials. Demand for tools that offer both efficiency and valid, balanced inference is high, as it translates to quicker product iterations, better resource allocation, and more confident business decisions.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{4. IMMEDIATE IDEAS FOR STARTUPS/PATENTS}\\
While the mathematical methods themselves might not be patentable, the implementation and commercial application of MADCovar and MADMod offer significant startup potential. A startup could develop a software-as-a-service (SaaS) platform providing advanced adaptive experimentation capabilities for data scientists and researchers, integrating these methods to offer superior precision and balanced power. This platform could include user-friendly interfaces, robust analytics dashboards, and seamless integration with existing data pipelines. Additionally, licensing the methodologies to established A/B testing platforms or enterprise analytics software providers represents a strong path for widespread adoption. The immediate next step is to productize the existing open-source software package into a scalable, commercially viable offering or develop targeted consulting services.

title: Trial Length, Pricing, and Rationally Inattentive Customers
abstract: The "free trial" followed by automatic renewal is a dominant business model in the digital economy. Standard models explain trials as a mechanism for consumers to learn their valuation for a product. We propose a complementary theory based on the rational inattention framework. Consumers know their valuation but face a cognitive cost to remember to cancel an unwanted subscription. We model this using a Shannon entropy-based cost of information processing, where a consumer's baseline attention level decays with the length of the trial period. This creates a novel trade-off for a monopolist firm: a longer trial increases "inattentive revenue" from consumers who fail to cancel, but it also lowers ex-ante consumer utility, making the initial offer less attractive. We show that this trade-off leads to an interior optimal trial length, even for products where value-learning is instantaneous. Our model, under standard assumptions about demand elasticity and the distribution of consumer valuations, generates sharp, testable predictions about the relationship between contract terms. We find that the optimal renewal price and trial length are complements: firms offering longer trials will also set higher post-trial prices. We analyze the impact of policies aimed at curbing consumer exploitation, such as "click-to-cancel" regulations. We show that such policies, by making attention effectively cheaper, lead firms to reduce trial lengths. The effect on price depends directly on the elasticity of demand from loyal subscribers. We also extend the model to include paid trials, showing that introductory prices and trial lengths act as strategic substitutes. Our framework provides a micro-founded explanation for common features of subscription contracts and offers a new lens through which to evaluate consumer protection policies in digital markets.
gemini_output:
\noindent\textbf{1. BACKGROUND \& CONTEXT}\\
This research explores the common "free trial" business model in the digital economy, focusing on how consumer inattention impacts its design. While traditional views suggest trials help customers learn product value, this study proposes a complementary theory: consumers face a cognitive cost to remember to cancel unwanted subscriptions. The work is crucial because it uses a rational inattention framework, based on Shannon entropy, to explain why trial lengths vary and how customer attention decays over time. This approach offers a deeper understanding of a pervasive business strategy beyond just product evaluation.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{2. REAL-WORLD PROBLEMS SOLVED}\\
The paper addresses a fundamental question for subscription businesses: why firms offer extended trials even when customers might instantly know a product's value. It reveals that firms face a trade-off: longer trials increase "inattentive revenue" from customers who forget to cancel, but they also reduce the initial appeal of the offer. This theoretical insight, at TRL 2 (concept formulated), clarifies how companies strategically balance these factors. For advancement, these predictions could be empirically tested using real-world subscription data to validate the model's accuracy.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{3. MARKET ANALYSIS}\\
The digital subscription market, encompassing streaming, software-as-a-service (SaaS), and apps, is vast and growing, making this research highly relevant. Industry demand exists for optimized pricing and trial strategies that maximize customer acquisition and retention. Current market players include a multitude of subscription services, all navigating these dynamics. However, firms face growing consumer protection concerns and regulations like "click-to-cancel" policies, which directly impact the effectiveness of inattention-based strategies. Collaborating with market analytics firms could help validate and apply these insights.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{4. IMMEDIATE IDEAS FOR STARTUPS/PATENTS}\\
This research, being a theoretical framework, is generally unpatentable. However, it offers significant insights for software development and consulting. Startups could create analytics platforms for subscription businesses, allowing them to model optimal trial lengths and pricing strategies based on estimated consumer inattention levels. Another opportunity lies in developing compliance tools that help firms adapt their offerings in response to "click-to-cancel" or similar regulations, predicting the impact on trial length and pricing. These findings could also be integrated into existing CRM or marketing automation software to refine customer onboarding and retention efforts.

title: Beyond pay: AI skills reward more job benefits
abstract: This study investigates the non-monetary rewards associated with artificial intelligence (AI) skills in the U.S. labour market. Using a dataset of approximately ten million online job vacancies from 2018 to 2024, we identify AI roles-positions requiring at least one AI-related skill-and examine the extent to which these roles offer non-monetary benefits such as tuition assistance, paid leave, health and well-being perks, parental leave, workplace culture enhancements, and remote work options. While previous research has documented substantial wage premiums for AI-related roles due to growing demand and limited talent supply, our study asks whether this demand also translates into enhanced non-monetary compensation. We find that AI roles are significantly more likely to offer such perks, even after controlling for education requirements, industry, and occupation type. It is twice as likely for an AI role to offer parental leave and almost three times more likely to provide remote working options. Moreover, the highest-paying AI roles tend to bundle these benefits, suggesting a compound premium where salary increases coincide with expanded non-monetary rewards. AI roles offering parental leave or health benefits show salaries that are, on average, 12% to 20% higher than AI roles without this benefit. This pattern is particularly pronounced in years and occupations experiencing the highest AI-related demand, pointing to a demand-driven dynamic. Our findings underscore the strong pull of AI talent in the labor market and challenge narratives of technological displacement, highlighting instead how employers compete for scarce talent through both financial and non-financial incentives.
gemini_output:
\noindent\textbf{1. BACKGROUND \& CONTEXT}\\
This research explores the non-monetary benefits associated with artificial intelligence (AI) skills in the U.S. job market, moving beyond the well-established wage premiums. The study analyzes roughly ten million online job vacancies from 2018 to 2024 to identify how often AI roles offer perks like tuition assistance, paid leave, health benefits, parental leave, and remote work. This investigation is crucial for understanding the full scope of employer competition for scarce AI talent, offering a more complete picture of compensation than salary alone.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{2. REAL-WORLD PROBLEMS SOLVED}\\
The paper addresses the challenge employers face in attracting and retaining top AI talent, revealing that non-monetary rewards are a significant part of the compensation strategy. It empirically demonstrates that AI roles are substantially more likely to offer these perks, with parental leave being twice as common and remote work options nearly three times more frequent than in non-AI roles. This insight is at TRL 3 (experimental proof of concept demonstrated), showing how employers are strategically bundling benefits to secure competitive advantage for high-demand AI positions. Further steps could involve validating these trends across different international markets.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{3. MARKET ANALYSIS}\\
The quantum computing market is emerging but niche; growth potential hinges on overcoming fundamental barriers like inverse access. Industry demand exists in quantum software (e.g., optimization tools) but startups face adoption challenges: high infrastructure costs and re-engineering classical systems. Competitors include existing quantum algorithms, but this work uniquely identifies inverse access as a bottleneck. Regulatory hurdles are minimal, though collaborations with quantum hardware firms (e.g., semiconductor companies) could accelerate TRL progression.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{4. IMMEDIATE IDEAS FOR STARTUPS/PATENTS}\\
This research, by identifying market trends, is not directly patentable. However, its findings are highly valuable for HR technology startups and talent analytics firms. A startup could develop a platform that provides data-driven insights into comprehensive compensation packages for AI roles, benchmarking non-monetary benefits against market leaders. This tool could help companies optimize their talent acquisition strategies by ensuring their offerings are competitive beyond just salary. A practical next step for established HR software providers is to integrate these findings into their talent management modules, enabling employers to design more attractive benefit structures for AI professionals.

title: Land and Infinite Debt Rollover
abstract: Since McCallum (1987), it is well known that in an overlapping generations (OLG) economy with land, the equilibrium is Pareto efficient because with balanced growth, the interest rate exceeds the economic growth rate ($R>G$), which rules out infinite debt rollover (a Ponzi scheme). We show that once we remove knife-edge restrictions on the production function and allow unbalanced growth, under some conditions an efficient equilibrium with land bubbles necessarily emerges and infinite debt rollover becomes possible, which is a markedly different insight from the conventional view derived from the Diamond (1965) landless economy. We also examine the possibility of Pareto inefficient equilibria.
gemini_output:
\noindent\textbf{1. BACKGROUND \& CONTEXT}\\
This research re-examines a core economic principle concerning debt sustainability in economies that include land. Traditionally, it was believed that land-rich economies naturally ensure efficient outcomes and prevent unsustainable "Ponzi schemes" (infinite debt rollover) because interest rates would outpace economic growth. This long-held view, stemming from Overlapping Generations (OLG) models, assumes specific conditions for economic growth and production. This study challenges that foundation by exploring what happens when these restrictive assumptions are relaxed, suggesting a more complex reality.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{2. REAL-WORLD PROBLEMS SOLVED}\\
The paper tackles a fundamental misunderstanding in economic theory about when economies can sustain infinite debt and experience asset bubbles, particularly for land. It proves that by allowing for more realistic economic conditions—like variable growth rates and flexible production—previously thought impossible situations, such as efficient economies with land bubbles and continuous debt rollover, can actually emerge. This theoretical breakthrough helps economists better understand the mechanisms behind asset price inflations and debt crises, moving beyond overly simplified models to explain real-world financial instability.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{3. MARKET ANALYSIS}\\
While not a direct product, this research provides crucial theoretical underpinnings for market analysis in economic policy and financial regulation. Demand comes from central banks, government treasuries, and international financial organizations needing to refine macroeconomic models for financial stability. Its primary impact is in improving the accuracy of economic forecasts, especially concerning asset bubbles and public debt sustainability. Adoption challenges involve integrating these complex theoretical insights into existing policy frameworks and convincing policymakers to revise long-standing assumptions.

\vspace{1em}

\noindent\textbf{4. IMMEDIATE IDEAS FOR STARTUPS/PATENTS}\\
This theoretical economic work is not patentable and does not directly lend itself to a startup product. However, its insights are valuable for informing policy and financial modeling tools. A practical next step would be for economic research institutions or financial advisory firms to integrate these refined conditions for land bubbles and debt rollover into their macroeconomic simulation software. This would enhance risk assessment for land-backed investments and debt management strategies, providing a more nuanced view for policymakers and investors.

title: Predicting Qualification Thresholds in UEFA's incomplete round-robin tournaments
abstract: For the 2024/25 season, the Union of European Football Associations (UEFA) introduced an incomplete round-robin format in the Champions League, Europa League, and Conference League, replacing the traditional group stage with a single league table of all 36 teams. Under this structure, the top eight teams advance directly to the round of 16, while those ranked 9th-24th compete in a play-off round. Simulation-based analyses, such as those by commercial data analyst Opta, provide indicative point thresholds for qualification but reveal deviations when compared with actual outcomes in the first season. To overcome these discrepancies, we employ a bivariate Dixon-Coles model that accounts for the lower frequency of draws observed in the 2024/25 UCL season, with team strengths proxied by Elo ratings. This framework enables the simulation of match outcomes and the estimation of qualification thresholds for both direct advancement and play-off participation. Our results provide scientific guidance for clubs and managers, supporting strategic decision-making under uncertainty regarding their progression prospects in the new UEFA club competition formats.
gemini_output:

The 2024/25 UEFA club competitions introduced a new, complex incomplete round-robin format, replacing traditional group stages with a single 36-team league. This shift creates significant uncertainty for clubs regarding the precise point thresholds needed for direct qualification or play-off spots. This research addresses this by developing a scientific method to predict these crucial qualification thresholds. It's vital because previous simulation-based analyses, like those from commercial providers, have shown inaccuracies, underscoring the need for a more robust predictive model.

The central problem solved is the lack of reliable, real-time qualification probability and threshold data for clubs navigating UEFA's new, less predictable league format. Current commercial models exhibit discrepancies, potentially leading clubs to make suboptimal strategic decisions. This research provides a refined bivariate Dixon-Coles model, accounting for observed game dynamics (like fewer draws) and using Elo ratings for team strengths, to offer more accurate predictions. At TRL 3 (experimental proof of concept), this enables clubs and managers to make scientifically guided decisions on tactics, player rotation, or transfer strategy under competitive uncertainty.

The sports analytics market, especially within elite football, has a strong demand for precise performance and outcome prediction tools. Professional clubs, media, and betting industries are key target audiences, currently relying on services from commercial data analysts like Opta. This research offers a distinct competitive advantage by directly addressing and improving upon the known inaccuracies of existing simulation models for the new UEFA format. Adoption challenges involve demonstrating sustained accuracy over multiple seasons and seamless integration with clubs' existing analytical frameworks.
